title: ASIC finds its teeth, hauls in record penalties
full_text:
Australia's corporate regulator amassed a record $830 million in civil penalties over the past financial year, including fines for major banks ANZ, HSBC and Westpac, after ramping up its investigations to drive a rise in criminal convictions and custodial sentences.
The penalty amount achieved by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission is bigger than the previous four years combined, indicating that the tougher approach to enforcement taken by former chair Joe Longo and his replacement Sarah Court is paying dividends.
The biggest single fine was the $300.2 million imposed on collapsed forex broker Union Standard International Group for what ASIC described as aggressive sales tactics that pressured "inexperienced and vulnerable people" into trading high-risk derivatives products.
Banks were also in the firing line. In December, the Federal Court added $10 million to ANZ's record $240 million fine following alleged misconduct in its retail and institutional divisions.
ANZ's widespread compliance failures included charging fees to dead customers and misreporting data related to the sale of $14 billion in government bonds.
ASIC was hauled over the coals during the banking royal commission in 2018, accused of being a "toothless tiger" for failing to take tougher action amid a litany of governance failings across the sector.
It has since lifted its game, with Longo presiding over an overhaul.
"Our enforcement work is focused on misconduct that causes real harm and we are delivering results, forcing change, strengthening accountability, and returning money to consumers and investors," said Court, who took over as chair from Longo on June 1.
"We are pursuing cases that expose serious failures in systems, governance and conduct, from scams and hardship failures to market infrastructure, superannuation, private credit, financial reporting and digital assets."
The $830 million in civil penalties orders for the year to June 30 eclipsed the $104.1 million ASIC reported in the 2024-25 financial year, although only $644 million has been paid into the public purse due to companies falling into liquidation and some fines being paid this financial year.
ASIC also secured a $35 million fine from HSBC Bank Australia over scam protection failures; Macquarie Securities was ordered to pay a $35 million penalty for systemic failures that led to the misreporting of millions of short sales and inaccurate market data; and Westpac was ordered to pay $26 million for widespread failures in responding to customer hardship requests.
Online retailer Walker Stores, which traded as Snaffle, was slapped with a $33.5 million penalty after being found to have overcharged consumers almost $20 million in excess interest, while Mercer Super was ordered to pay $10.3 million in penalties for systemic reporting failures. ASIC initiated more than 250 investigations, roughly in line with the previous year, but over the past four years it has doubled the number of cases it looks into. Prosecutions resulted in 25 criminal convictions being recorded against individuals, up from 19 convictions in the 2024-25 financial year.
Among ASIC's high-profile victories was the probe into disgraced Sydney fund manager Rodney Forrest, who remains behind bars after pleading guilty to two counts of insider trading in the shares of Platinum Asset Management, the fund of investing veteran Kerr Neilson.
"ASIC has delivered record penalties and strong criminal outcomes, but enforcement is not just about punishment. It is about detecting misconduct sooner, preventing harm where we can, and securing remediation for those affected," Court said.
"Our focus is on protecting investors, returning money where possible, and holding lawbreakers to account. Where we see serious harm or risks to market integrity, we will act quickly and use the full range of regulatory and enforcement tools available to us."
